stem: An administrator performs a full backup on Sunday and incremental backups each night after. To restore data lost Thursday morning, which sets are needed?

options.text: The Sunday full plus every incremental from Monday through Wednesday
options.rationale: Incremental restore requires the last full plus every subsequent incremental in order, since each captures only changes since the prior backup.

options.text: Only Wednesday's incremental
options.rationale: A single incremental holds only that day's changes, not the full data set; restoring it alone is insufficient.

options.text: Only the Sunday full
options.rationale: The full alone misses all changes made Monday through Wednesday.

options.text: The Sunday full plus only Wednesday's incremental
options.rationale: Skipping Monday and Tuesday incrementals would omit changes those days captured.

stem: A full backup runs Sunday and differential backups run each night. To restore Thursday morning, which sets are needed?

options.text: The Sunday full plus only Wednesday night's differential
options.rationale: Differential restore needs just the last full plus the most recent single differential, which contains all changes since the full.

options.text: The Sunday full plus every differential from Monday to Wednesday
options.rationale: Differentials are cumulative since the full, so only the latest one is needed, not all of them.

options.text: Only Wednesday's differential
options.rationale: The differential alone lacks the baseline data in the full backup.

options.text: Only the Sunday full
options.rationale: The full alone misses all changes since Sunday captured by the differential.

stem: A team wants the fastest possible nightly backup window and accepts a more complex restore. Which backup type is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Incremental, because it copies only changes since the last backup
options.rationale: Incrementals are the smallest and fastest to create, at the cost of a longer, more complex multi-set restore.

options.text: Full, because it is simplest to restore
options.rationale: Full backups are the slowest and largest to create, contradicting the fastest-window requirement.

options.text: Differential, because it never grows
options.rationale: Differentials grow each day until the next full and take longer to create than incrementals.

options.text: No backup at all
options.rationale: Skipping backups leaves no recovery capability and is never appropriate.

stem: A critical system must resume within a couple of hours of a disaster with minimal data loss. Which alternate site strategy BEST meets this?

options.text: A hot site, fully equipped and continuously updated
options.rationale: A hot site enables recovery in minutes to hours with current data, matching a tight RTO and low RPO.

options.text: A cold site
options.rationale: A cold site takes weeks to become operational, far exceeding a two-hour RTO.

options.text: A reciprocal agreement with a partner firm
options.rationale: Reciprocal agreements are cheap but often lack the capacity and guaranteed readiness for a tight RTO on a critical system.

options.text: No alternate site at all
options.rationale: Without an alternate site, a facility loss would prevent recovery within the required window.

stem: A low-priority system can tolerate weeks of downtime, and cost is the main constraint. Which alternate site is BEST suited?

options.text: A cold site with only space, power, and cooling
options.rationale: A cold site is the cheapest option and its weeks-long readiness is acceptable for a system that tolerates long downtime.

options.text: A hot site
options.rationale: A hot site is the most expensive and unnecessary for a system that tolerates weeks of downtime.

options.text: A fully staffed duplicate data center
options.rationale: A duplicate staffed center is the costliest approach, contrary to the cost constraint.

options.text: Continuous real-time replication to two hot sites
options.rationale: Dual hot-site replication is far more expensive than needed for a low-priority system.

stem: A team believes its RAID 5 array is its backup. A user accidentally deletes a critical folder and it is gone from the array. What does this MOST clearly demonstrate?

options.text: RAID provides fault tolerance against disk failure but is not a backup and does not protect against deletion or corruption
options.rationale: RAID keeps a system running through a drive failure but immediately reflects deletions and corruption, so it cannot substitute for backups.

options.text: RAID automatically restores deleted files
options.rationale: RAID does not version or retain deleted data; the deletion propagates across the array.

options.text: RAID protects against ransomware and site loss
options.rationale: RAID offers no protection against corruption, ransomware, or destruction of the whole site.

options.text: RAID makes offsite backups unnecessary
options.rationale: Because RAID is not backup, offsite backups remain essential.

stem: A database must be recoverable with only seconds to minutes of potential data loss. Which data-protection method BEST achieves this fine-grained recovery point?

options.text: Remote journaling that continuously transmits transaction logs offsite
options.rationale: Streaming transaction logs continuously yields a much better RPO than periodic batch backups, enabling near-real-time recovery.

options.text: Nightly electronic vaulting of full backups
options.rationale: Batch nightly vaulting can lose up to a day of data, far exceeding a seconds-to-minutes RPO.

options.text: Weekly full backups to tape
options.rationale: Weekly tape backups could lose up to a week of transactions, grossly exceeding the requirement.

options.text: Manual monthly exports
options.rationale: Monthly manual exports provide an extremely poor RPO, unacceptable here.

stem: Which is the LEAST reliable characteristic of a reciprocal (mutual aid) agreement for disaster recovery?

options.text: Its dependability, because the partner may lack spare capacity and the arrangement is hard to enforce
options.rationale: Reciprocal agreements are cheap but often unreliable due to capacity, confidentiality, and enforceability concerns.

options.text: Its low cost
options.rationale: Low cost is actually the main advantage of reciprocal agreements, not their weakness.

options.text: Its informal familiarity between partners
options.rationale: Familiarity is a minor benefit, not the least reliable characteristic.

options.text: Its avoidance of new facility leases
options.rationale: Avoiding new leases is a cost benefit, not the reliability weakness.

stem: Which backup type copies all selected data every time and is simplest to restore from a single set?

options.text: Full backup
options.rationale: A full backup copies everything each run, so restoration uses just that one set.

options.text: Incremental backup
options.rationale: An incremental copies only recent changes and requires multiple sets to restore.

options.text: Differential backup
options.rationale: A differential copies changes since the last full and needs the full plus itself to restore.

options.text: Snapshot-only backup
options.rationale: A point-in-time snapshot is not the described full-copy scheme and often depends on the underlying volume.

stem: What PRIMARILY determines which recovery strategy an organization should select for a given system?

options.text: The system's required RTO and RPO, balanced against cost
options.rationale: Recovery strategies are chosen to meet the defined recovery time and recovery point objectives at acceptable cost.

options.text: The brand of the server hardware
options.rationale: Hardware branding does not drive recovery strategy selection.

options.text: The number of employees who like the system
options.rationale: Popularity is irrelevant to recovery objectives.

options.text: The color of the data center walls
options.rationale: This is unrelated to recovery strategy decisions.

stem: An organization prioritizes the fastest and simplest restore process even if nightly backups take longer. Between incremental and differential, which is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Differential, because restore needs only the last full plus one differential
options.rationale: Differential backups restore from just two sets, giving a faster, simpler restore than incrementals' many-set chain.

options.text: Incremental, because restore is simplest
options.rationale: Incremental restore is the most complex, needing the full plus every increment in sequence.

options.text: Incremental, because it uses only one set to restore
options.rationale: Incremental restore requires multiple sets, not one.

options.text: Neither can be restored
options.rationale: Both can be restored; the question is which restore is faster and simpler.

stem: Which statement BEST describes how the archive bit behaves for incremental versus differential backups?

options.text: Incremental clears the archive bit; differential does not clear it
options.rationale: Incrementals clear the bit so only new changes are captured next time; differentials leave it set so they accumulate changes since the last full.

options.text: Both clear the archive bit
options.rationale: Only incremental clears it; differential leaves it set, which is why differentials grow.

options.text: Neither interacts with the archive bit
options.rationale: Both backup types are defined in part by their handling of the archive bit.

options.text: Differential clears the archive bit; incremental does not
options.rationale: This reverses the correct behavior.

stem: A system can tolerate a day or two of downtime, and the organization wants a middle ground between cost and recovery speed. Which alternate site BEST fits?

options.text: A warm site with hardware and connectivity but not current data
options.rationale: A warm site balances cost and recovery time, coming online in hours to days, which fits the tolerance.

options.text: A hot site that is fully current at all times
options.rationale: A hot site exceeds the need and cost for a system tolerating a day or two of downtime.

options.text: A cold site taking weeks to activate
options.rationale: A cold site's weeks-long readiness exceeds the one-to-two-day tolerance.

options.text: No recovery site of any kind
options.rationale: Having no site risks exceeding the tolerated downtime entirely.

stem: Which ordering correctly ranks alternate sites from fastest/most expensive to slowest/cheapest recovery?

options.text: Hot, warm, cold
options.rationale: Hot sites recover fastest at highest cost, warm sites are intermediate, and cold sites are slowest and cheapest.

options.text: Cold, warm, hot
options.rationale: This reverses the order; cold is slowest and cheapest, not fastest.

options.text: Warm, hot, cold
options.rationale: Hot, not warm, is the fastest and most expensive.

options.text: Cold, hot, warm
options.rationale: This ordering is incorrect for both speed and cost.

stem: Which statement BEST captures the role of RAID in a recovery strategy?

options.text: RAID provides fault tolerance so a system survives a disk failure, but it is not a substitute for backups
options.rationale: RAID mitigates drive failure but does not protect against deletion, corruption, or site loss, so backups remain necessary.

options.text: RAID replaces the need for any backups
options.rationale: RAID is not backup and does not protect against many data-loss scenarios.

options.text: RAID protects data from ransomware corruption
options.rationale: RAID reflects corrupted writes across the array; it does not protect against ransomware.

options.text: RAID recovers data after the entire site is destroyed
options.rationale: RAID is local; it offers no protection if the whole site is lost.

stem: An organization wants to automatically send its batched backups to a remote facility on a schedule for offsite protection. Which method BEST describes this?

options.text: Electronic vaulting
options.rationale: Electronic vaulting transmits batched backup data to a remote location on a scheduled basis.

options.text: Remote journaling
options.rationale: Remote journaling continuously streams transaction logs, not scheduled batch backups.

options.text: RAID striping
options.rationale: RAID striping distributes data across local disks and is not offsite transmission.

options.text: Degaussing
options.rationale: Degaussing erases magnetic media and is unrelated to offsite backup transmission.

stem: A utility needs a self-contained, transportable processing facility that can be moved to a disaster area. Which option BEST describes this?

options.text: A mobile site
options.rationale: A mobile site is a transportable, self-contained facility that can be relocated to where it is needed.

options.text: A cold site
options.rationale: A cold site is fixed, empty space, not a transportable unit.

options.text: A reciprocal agreement
options.rationale: A reciprocal agreement is a mutual-hosting arrangement, not a physical transportable facility.

options.text: A RAID array
options.rationale: A RAID array is disk fault tolerance, not a processing facility.

stem: Which backup scheme, all else equal, is LEAST convenient when the priority is a quick, low-complexity restore?

options.text: Incremental backups
options.rationale: Incremental restore requires the last full plus every subsequent increment in order, making it the most complex and least convenient to restore.

options.text: Full backups
options.rationale: Full backups restore from a single set, the most convenient restore.

options.text: Differential backups
options.rationale: Differential restore needs only the full plus one differential, more convenient than incrementals.

options.text: A full backup followed by a single differential
options.rationale: This two-set restore is convenient, not the least convenient option.

stem: A system's RPO allows up to 24 hours of data loss and its RTO allows a full day of downtime. Which recovery approach is BEST aligned to these relaxed objectives at lower cost?

options.text: Nightly backups with electronic vaulting to a warm or cold arrangement
options.rationale: Relaxed 24-hour objectives are satisfied by nightly offsite backups at lower cost than continuous replication and hot sites.

options.text: Continuous synchronous replication to a hot site
options.rationale: Continuous replication and a hot site are overbuilt and costly for objectives that tolerate a day of loss and downtime.

options.text: Sub-second failover clustering
options.rationale: Sub-second failover far exceeds and overspends for a 24-hour RPO/RTO.

options.text: No backup strategy at all
options.rationale: No strategy means potentially unlimited data loss, failing even relaxed objectives.

stem: Why might an organization choose weekly full backups combined with daily incrementals rather than daily full backups?

options.text: To minimize daily backup time and storage while accepting a longer restore chain
options.rationale: Full-plus-incremental reduces the size and duration of daily backups, trading off a more complex restore for efficiency.

options.text: To make each daily backup as large as possible
options.rationale: Incrementals are chosen precisely to keep daily backups small, not large.

options.text: To eliminate the need for any full backup
options.rationale: A periodic full backup is still required as the base of the restore chain.

options.text: To guarantee zero data loss with no backups
options.rationale: This is contradictory; backups are what enable recovery, and the scheme still has an RPO.
